At nine on Monday morning, the council hired me to remove a doorway from the town hall.

“The whole wall?” I asked.

“Just the doorway,” said Mrs. Vale. “People keep going through it.”

This seemed to me the strongest argument in the doorway’s favor, but I had recently become self-employed and was learning which thoughts belonged on an invoice.

The doorway connected the records office to a narrow courtyard. It had no door, only two iron hinges painted so many times they resembled small white fists. On the other side stood a bench, a drain, and a pear tree. The pears were hard and yellow and, according to a handwritten notice, not for eating.

I set down my toolbox. A man in a bicycle helmet came through carrying a mug.

“Morning,” he said.

“Morning. Where are you headed?”

“Accounts.”

“Is Accounts out here?”

“No,” he said, and sat on the bench.

By eleven I’d counted seventeen crossings. A woman from Licensing came out to practice saying something under her breath. A boy delivered an envelope to the records clerk and took the long way back past the tree. Two cleaners met in the courtyard and exchanged shoes. I waited for an explanation. None came.

Mrs. Vale appeared at noon. “How are we getting on?”

“I’m trying to understand the scope of the work.”

“Brick it up.”

“People seem to like it.”

“They do. Unfortunately, the plans say there’s a wall here. The insurer has noticed.”

“Could you change the plans?”

She rubbed the bridge of her nose. “You must be new to contracting.”

That evening, at home, I told my daughter about the doorway. She was eight and sorting a tin of buttons into families according to rules she would not disclose.

“Where will the people go instead?” she asked.

“Back to work, I suppose.”

“No, I mean the ones who need to go through.”

I explained that nobody needed to go through. The courtyard led nowhere. There was another entrance by the bins for anyone who needed access to the drain or the tree.

She considered this. “Maybe nowhere is where they need to go.”

Then she held up a green button with a chip missing from one edge. “This one’s a grandfather.”

On Tuesday I brought bricks. The man in the bicycle helmet helped me unload them.

“Bit of a shame,” he said.

“What do you do out there?”

“Drink my tea.”

“Couldn’t you drink it at your desk?”

“I could drink it in the bath. But then I’d be a man who drinks office tea in the bath.”

We carried the bricks in silence after that.

I laid the first course before lunch. People stepped over it. By two, they had to lift their knees. By four, the woman from Licensing stood on one side and finished her sentence on the other.

“What was it you needed to say?” I asked.

“‘I won’t be available on Saturdays.’”

“Did it help?”

“I’ve got Saturday off.”

On Wednesday, the wall reached my waist. The cleaners came, looked at it, and exchanged shoes across the top.

“All right,” I said. “I’ve got to ask.”

One of them pointed down. She wore a black orthopedic boot on her left foot. The other wore an identical boot on her right. They had bought one expensive pair of shoes between them and took turns wearing the new one on the foot that could wear it.

“We’re breaking them in for our sister’s wedding,” one said.

“We’re both hoping to be better by June,” said the other.

On Thursday, I finished. I raked the joints, swept the floor, and painted the plaster on the office side a pale municipal cream. Unless you knew where to look, you would never suspect there had been a way through.

Mrs. Vale signed the invoice.

I went outside by the bins to collect my tools. From the courtyard, the new brickwork looked raw and rather handsome. The pear tree dropped a pear. It hit the bench with a wooden knock.

I picked it up and took a bite. It was like biting a table.

“Needs cooking,” said Mrs. Vale behind me.

“What about the notice?”

“I put that up after the clerk cracked a crown.”

She had brought a shopping bag. Together we gathered the pears that came away easily. She said she poached them with lemon peel and packed them into jars. Every December she gave the jars to people she had annoyed during the year.

“Do you have enough pears?” I asked.

“Not remotely.”

The council paid me in thirty days. A month after that, Mrs. Vale called again.

“We need a bench,” she said.

“For the courtyard?”

“For the corridor. Outside Records.”

I built it in oak, long enough for three people who knew one another or two who didn’t. The man in the bicycle helmet sat down before I’d packed away my drill. He set his mug beside him. Someone had drawn a small, convincing pear on it in green ink.

By winter, the cream paint above the bench had acquired a dark patch where people rested their heads. The woman from Licensing brought in a cushion. One of the cleaners left a wedding photograph on the windowsill: both sisters standing in silver shoes, their arms around a third woman laughing so hard her veil had slipped over one eye.

And in December a jar appeared on my doorstep. The pears inside were almost transparent. Tied around the lid was a note from Mrs. Vale.

*For the inconvenience.*

My daughter and I ate them warm, over toast. She fished the last strip of lemon peel from the syrup and held it up to the light.

“What’s that bit for?” she asked.

I thought of the bench, the doorway, the courtyard on the other side.

“Try it,” I said.
